1.title: Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective
1.text: Welcome to Module 9: Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. These two events close every Sprint. The Review looks at the product, and the Retrospective looks at how the team works. In this module you will learn what each one is for, how to run them, and what a team loses if it skips the Retrospective.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose, participants and timebox of the Review and of the Retrospective. Perform a Sprint Review. Perform a Sprint Retrospective. Give three effects of skipping the Retrospective. Tell the two events apart. And spot the traps: the Review treated as a gate, and the Review treated as a demo for approval.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Sign-Off in Disguise
1.text: At the end of Sprint seven, Grace Whitfield arrives at the Review with a checklist and asks the team to sign the Sprint off. Two items are almost done, but not Done. The Retrospective comes next, and the same complaints about the slow station map keep returning. As Scrum Master, you prepare to explain what both events are really for. Grace's checklist and the almost-done items will both come back in this module.

1.title: The Sprint Review
1.text: First the Sprint Review. Its purpose is to examine the outcome of the Sprint and decide what to adapt next. The Scrum Team and key stakeholders attend. Together they look at what was accomplished and what has changed around the product, and then agree the next steps together. The Product Backlog may change to catch new opportunities. It is a working session, not just a presentation. It is the second to last event, and takes four hours at most for a one-month Sprint.

1.title: What Is Shown, and What Is Not
1.text: What is shown at the Review? The Increments of the Sprint are presented there. But an Increment may be delivered earlier than the Review, so the Review is never a gate to releasing value. And here is the key rule. An item that misses the Definition of Done is neither released nor shown at the Review. It returns to the Product Backlog. So Grace's almost-done items stay out of the demonstration, however good they look. And Grace's checklist cannot turn the Review into a sign-off: it is a working session about what to do next, not an approval gate.

1.title: Performing a Sprint Review
1.text: How do you perform a Sprint Review? The Guide describes the event, and the steps are good practice, so this slide goes beyond the Guide. Before: invite the key stakeholders, and check what meets the Definition of Done. Open with the purpose, the timebox and the Sprint Goal. Show what is Done, and say what is not. Discuss progress toward the Product Goal and what has changed around the product. Collaborate on what to do next. Then the Product Owner adjusts the Product Backlog, and you close on time.

1.title: Who Decides at the Review?
1.text: Who decides at the Review? Stakeholders give feedback and ideas, but they do not order the Product Backlog. The Product Owner decides how to adjust it. The Scrum Team presents what is Done. And the Scrum Master helps stakeholder collaboration when asked or needed. If a stakeholder wants a new feature first, the route is the same as always: convince the Product Owner.

1.title: Inspect and Adapt at the Review
1.text: The learning objective asks for an example of inspecting and adapting at each event. This one goes beyond the Guide. At the Review, the team inspects the Increment and what has changed in the environment. It adapts when the Product Owner reorders the Product Backlog after the feedback. The transparency gained: everyone sees the real state of the product and of the Product Goal.

1.title: Review Traps
1.text: The Review traps. It is a working session, not a one-way presentation or a status report. It is not a gate, because work can be delivered earlier. What is not Done is not shown, and returns to the Product Backlog. Stakeholders advise, and the Product Owner adjusts the Product Backlog. And in the earlier edition, the Review was called an informal meeting with target dates; treat that as old wording. Never present unfinished work just to look good.

1.title: The Sprint Retrospective
1.text: The purpose of the Retrospective is to plan ways to raise quality and effectiveness. The team then looks at how the Sprint went: individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done. It discusses what went well, what problems arose, and how they were or were not solved, and it looks at assumptions that misled the team. The output is the most helpful changes. The biggest ones are tackled right away, and may enter the next Sprint Backlog. The event concludes the Sprint, with three hours at most.

1.title: Performing a Sprint Retrospective
1.text: How do you perform a Retrospective? Again, this goes beyond the Guide. Set the stage: restate the purpose and rules, and create a safe, open atmosphere. Gather data: what happened, what went well, what caused problems. Generate insights by asking why, and which assumptions misled the team. Decide: choose the few most helpful changes and make each concrete. Close: add the most impactful improvement to the next Sprint Backlog. Formats such as start, stop, continue are only examples.

1.title: Effects of Skipping the Retrospective
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three effects of skipping the Retrospective. This list goes beyond the Guide, but follows from its warning that skipping any event loses a chance to inspect and adapt. Problems repeat. There is no improvement, because the one event planned for it is gone. Wrong assumptions stay hidden. Trust and openness erode. Morale and ownership fall. And the Definition of Done stalls. That is what happened at RideLoop with the station map.

1.title: Review and Retrospective Compared
1.text: Compare the two events. The Review inspects the outcome, with the Scrum Team and key stakeholders, adapts the Product Backlog, and lasts four hours at most. The Retrospective inspects the way of working, with the Scrum Team alone, adapts the team's practices, and lasts three hours at most. A simple way to remember: the Review asks, what did we build, and what next? The Retrospective asks, how did we work, and how can we do better?

1.title: Retrospective Traps
1.text: The Retrospective traps. It concludes the Sprint; it comes after the Review, not before the next Planning. It is for the Scrum Team only, and managers belong at the Review. The biggest improvements are tackled right away. Skipping it loses the planned chance to improve, and the best answer restores it. The Scrum Master takes part as a member. In the earlier edition you will find a peer team member and a mandatory process improvement item; that is old wording. The tip: the Retrospective inspects people, process, tools and the Definition of Done, not the Increment.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and adjusts the Product Backlog. The Retrospective plans improvements and concludes the Sprint. The timeboxes are four hours and three hours at most. Not Done is never presented, and returns to the Product Backlog. Skipping the Retrospective means problems repeat and nothing improves. Both events are formal chances to inspect and adapt. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The RideLoop team plans a one-hour slide presentation for the Sprint Review and does not expect any questions. What should the Scrum Master advise? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The Review is meant to be a working session, and a one-way presentation misses its point. Attendees collaborate on what to do next, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. At the Sprint seven Review, Grace wants to see an item that is almost done but does not yet meet the Definition of Done, so that progress can be seen. What should happen? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The item cannot be presented or released, and it returns to the Product Backlog. Lowering the Definition of Done for one item would undermine transparency.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A senior Lakeshore Transit manager asks to attend every RideLoop Retrospective to hear what the team's problems are. What is the best response from the Scrum Master? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The Retrospective is the Scrum Team's own inspection of its way of working, and openness needs a safe setting. The manager's interest can be served at the Review.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. What does the Scrum Team inspect in the Sprint Retrospective? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B: individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done. The Product Backlog and the Increment are inspected at the Review, and individual performance for managers is not the purpose.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which of these is an effect of skipping the Sprint Retrospective? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. The same problems keep returning, because the one event for improving the way of working is gone. Skipping it does not change the Sprint length, the Product Owner's authority, or the Review.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. The Review is a working session. Question two: D. Work that misses the Definition of Done is not presented. Question three: C. The Retrospective is the Scrum Team's own inspection. Question four: B. People, process, tools and the Definition of Done. Question five: B. Problems repeat. That completes Module 9. Next, Module 10 covers the Product Backlog, the Product Goal and refinement.
